summary: Terra Analog is a regional terrain-comparison prototype for exploring where measured Earth topography falls within selected terrain profiles for Jezero crater on Mars or the Moon's south polar region. Users choose a profile, one to three criteria with positive weights, a named Earth region and either an individual-pixel Top 10 or a distinct-area ranking with a stated minimum separation. The application returns individual candidate cells, maps the results and explains the selected pixel's measurements and score contributions. It compares topographic features only. It does not establish a complete environmental analogue, habitability or a mission site recommendation.
details:
Terra Analog is a regional terrain-comparison prototype created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It helps users explore where measured Earth terrain falls within selected topographic profiles for Jezero crater on Mars or the lunar south polar region. A user chooses a planetary profile, an Earth region, active measurements and positive weights, then inspects ranked Earth cells and the measurements behind a selected result.

The prototype compares three terrain features:

- Surface slope, in degrees

- Local topographic roughness, in metres, calculated from elevation residuals after removing a local plane

- Local topographic relief, in metres, calculated as the 95th percentile minus the 5th percentile of local elevation

The Earth search uses versioned 2 km analysis cells with a nominal area of 4 km² and a 10 km physical neighbourhood for terrain features. Earth elevation comes from NOAA ETOPO 2022 at 15 arc seconds, approximately 0.42 to 0.46 km per source posting in these study regions. A GSHHG land mask keeps ocean bathymetry out of land-terrain measurements. OpenStreetMap provides geographic context and is not included in the score.

NASA MOLA data define the Jezero reference profile. NASA LOLA Product 90 defines the lunar south polar profile. The method compares terrain derivatives at stated scales and does not compare absolute elevations across different planetary reference systems.

Each feature interval is an area-weighted P10 to P90 range from its selected profile. An experimental tolerance of 1.5 times the profile feature's interquartile range is used outside that interval. Active feature weights are normalized. A score of 100 means the selected cell's active measurements fall inside their reference intervals. It is an experimental similarity index, not a probability, habitability estimate or complete environmental analogue verdict.

Every eligible Earth cell is scored individually before map aggregation. The Top 10 pixel ranking preserves nearby high-scoring cells. A separate distinct-areas mode selects representatives with an explicit minimum separation. Missing measurements remain unavailable with a reason and are not treated as zero.

The local Live API returned these regional results:

Mars, Jezero profile against Atacama / Andes:

1,791 of 1,796 cells were eligible, or 99.72 percent. The selected 4 km² pixel scored 100 percent. Its slope was 5.52 degrees against a Jezero interval of 0.38 to 5.68 degrees. Its roughness was 161.68 m against 20.66 to 175.21 m. Its relief was 694.22 m against 138.33 to 887.63 m.

Moon, lunar 80 to 90 degrees south profile against Hawaii Big Island:

1,497 of 1,854 cells were eligible, or 80.74 percent. The selected 4 km² pixel scored 100 percent. Its slope was 4.76 degrees against a lunar interval of 1.28 to 14.39 degrees. Its roughness was 115.52 m against 115.06 to 452.24 m. Its relief was 1,338.82 m against 572.22 to 2,959.49 m.

These are regional results, not a global search or global optimum. The prototype scores topography only. It does not assess climate, illumination, radiation, atmosphere, water, geology, mineralogy or biological suitability. Similar topography does not show that two locations have matching materials or are suitable for a mission. The web application has been tested locally and is not publicly deployed.

The application uses Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, Rasterio, pyproj, Uvicorn, React, MapLibre GL JS, Vite and TypeScript.

OpenAI Codex assisted with parts of the data-acquisition, terrain-processing, scoring and web-application code, source checks, English editing and this presentation. The team set the goals and reviewed the work. The measurements shown came from cited source data processed by deterministic code. AI did not generate or modify the measurement observations. The images in the presentation are application screenshots and map tiles, not AI-generated images. No AI-generated audio or video is used.
